strengths: The paper addresses a practically relevant and comparatively underexplored problem: reconstructing sharp, animatable 3D human Gaussian avatars directly from motion-blurred multi-view video.

The proposed differentiable blur-formation pipeline is well motivated: it renders a sequence of SMPL-deformed canonical Gaussians and averages the resulting sharp images, allowing avatar appearance and sub-frame motion to be optimized jointly.

The evaluation reports large and consistent gains over direct GauHuman training and four deblur-then-reconstruct baselines. On the synthetic benchmark, the method improves PSNR from approximately 23.1 to 25.55 and LPIPS from approximately 0.22 to 0.148; gains also persist on the real captures and under stronger synthetic blur.

The synchronized real capture system, containing four long-exposure and eight short-exposure cameras across eight scenes, is a useful contribution because it permits evaluation using real motion blur and sharp novel-view references.

Ablations cover pose interpolation, non-rigid displacement, LBS and shape refinement, inter-frame regularization, blur magnitude, knot count, and temporal sample count. In particular, the non-middle-timestep experiment provides useful evidence that inter-frame regularization resolves some motion-direction ambiguity.
weaknesses: The central claim of recovering sub-frame human motion is not adequately validated. The paper provides no joint-angle, keypoint, mesh, or trajectory error against known motion on the synthetic data. Image metrics can improve through appearance/geometry compensation without establishing that the inferred sub-frame poses are correct, especially given the inherent non-identifiability of time-averaged observations.

The baseline study does not isolate the attainable reconstruction quality or the source of the gains. An oracle GauHuman model trained on the corresponding sharp frames is missing, so the remaining gap to sharp-input reconstruction is unknown. Results are also only aggregated over six synthetic subjects and eight real scenes, without per-sequence statistics, variance, or significance estimates.

Important experimental details needed for reproducibility are absent: architectures and inputs of the pose-displacement and LBS-offset networks, initialization of sub-frame control poses, training schedule and iteration count, loss normalization or weighting, Gaussian densification settings, and exposure-window alignment are not specified. The manuscript says that code and data are public but supplies no accessible location in the provided paper.

The motion formulation has technical ambiguities. Although joint rotations are described as elements of SO(3), Equations 11–14 interpolate and add three-dimensional pose vectors in Euclidean space without explaining the rotation representation or manifold handling. Equation 10 uses t/T while discrete samples run through T-1, and the stated 'B-spline' construction and boundary behavior are insufficiently explained.

The synthetic blur protocol is unclear: the text says five consecutive frames are averaged, while also inserting eight RIFE frames between every adjacent pair and averaging the interpolated frames. This does not clearly match the five-sample forward model used by the method and introduces interpolation artifacts that may favor a smooth trajectory model.

The real-data protocol needs stronger controls. Blur and sharp targets come from different cameras, so reported scores conflate deblurring with novel-view synthesis and may be affected by camera response, color calibration, and exposure timing; only an ND filter and nominal exposure ratio are described. No direct verification of radiometric or temporal alignment is reported.

The physical model averages rendered RGB values uniformly and does not discuss linear radiance, camera response, shutter weighting, or foreground-background visibility integration. The authors acknowledge that preprocessing masks discard the boundary blending caused by motion blur, which is a substantive limitation for exactly the observations being modeled.

Presentation issues reduce confidence but are secondary to the evidence gaps: the image/video-deblurring related-work paragraph is nearly duplicated, dataset resolution is inconsistent between Table 1 and the prose, several symbols change roles or dimensions, and the title's 'bundle adjusted' terminology is not clearly connected to a defined bundle-adjustment objective.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically relevant and underexplored problem: reconstructing sharp, animatable 3D human avatars from motion-blurred multi-view video.

The central formulation is coherent and physically motivated: sub-frame SMPL-conditioned Gaussian renderings are averaged over the exposure interval, allowing avatar appearance and motion trajectories to be jointly optimized.
The real dataset uses synchronized cameras with different exposure settings, while the synthetic benchmark enables controlled evaluation. This is a potentially useful contribution to the community.

Reported gains are substantial on both benchmarks: approximately 2.5 dB PSNR over the strongest baseline on synthetic data and 1.4 dB on real data. The component, blur-magnitude, temporal-regularization, control-knot, and sampling ablations are useful and generally support the design choices.
The manuscript is mostly understandable, and the figures communicate the reconstruction improvements and the foreground-background blending limitation reasonably well.
weaknesses: The comparison set is not sufficient to establish the claimed superiority of the joint formulation. All principal baselines use GauHuman, either directly or after generic 2D video deblurring. There is no sharp-frame oracle, no comparison to alternative Gaussian-avatar backbones, and no adapted joint multi-view deblurring method. Declaring existing NeRF/3DGS deblurring methods inapplicable does not replace an experimental comparison or a carefully matched adaptation.

The evidence for recovering correct sub-frame motion is incomplete. Most metrics evaluate rendered sharp images, and even the non-middle-timestep experiment measures image quality rather than pose or trajectory error. Given the fundamental motion-direction and inverse-rendering ambiguities discussed by the paper itself, good rendered images do not demonstrate that the recovered motion is physically correct.

The real-data evaluation is small—eight scenes—with no per-scene results, variance, repeated runs, or statistical analysis. The paper also does not characterize motion types, speeds, clothing, or subject diversity, so robustness and generalization beyond this particular capture rig remain unclear.

The synthetic benchmark depends on RIFE-generated intermediate frames and averaging consecutive ZJU-MoCap frames. Consequently, success may partly reflect the interpolation model's artifacts and a blur-generation process closely matched to the proposed renderer. No evaluation tests mismatched exposure functions, nonlinear camera response, rolling shutter, or naturally occurring blur outside the authors' controlled rig.

Important implementation details are missing: the architectures of the pose-displacement and LBS-offset networks, initialization of spline controls and Gaussian/avatar parameters, training iterations, loss weighting, masking details, densification schedule, and complete learning-rate settings. Saying settings follow 3DGS is insufficient for reproducing a substantially different joint optimization procedure. Runtime and memory costs from rendering multiple sub-frames are also absent.

The motion parameterization is technically under-justified. Joint rotations described as elements of SO(3) are interpolated and additively displaced in a Euclidean three-vector representation, without explaining the rotation representation, conversion, or handling of wraparound and manifold geometry. This matters for high-amplitude motion and for the claim of plausible sub-frame trajectories.

Precomputed hard masks cannot represent the fractional foreground coverage created by motion blur. The paper acknowledges this limitation, but it directly affects the assumed image-formation model and may bias both training and evaluation around moving boundaries; no quantitative sensitivity analysis is provided.

Several results attributed to individual components are very small—for example, shape optimization changes real-data PSNR from 26.964 to 27.010 and LPIPS from 0.1669 to 0.1668—yet are interpreted as definitive without uncertainty estimates.

Reproducibility is further weakened by inconsistent capture specifications: Table 1 reports 2448×2048 resolution, whereas the dataset description reports 2080×2048. Dataset/code availability is asserted without sufficient release, split, calibration, or licensing details in the manuscript.

Presentation issues are secondary but noticeable: the image/video deblurring related-work discussion is largely duplicated, notation reuses R for both rasterization and camera extrinsics, the loss omits an explicit regularization coefficient, and numerous grammatical errors and imprecise claims reduce clarity. These could be corrected editorially, but the baseline coverage and motion-validation deficiencies are material.

strengths: The paper addresses a practical and relatively underexplored problem: reconstructing sharp, animatable 3D Gaussian human avatars directly from motion-blurred multi-view videos. Jointly estimating sub-frame human motion and a canonical avatar is a meaningful contribution to vision and graphics. The method is coherent and technically motivated: SMPL-based deformation, spline-constrained sub-frame poses, learnable residual motion, and temporal regularization reduce the ambiguities of optimizing independent latent sharp frames, while averaging rendered sub-frames provides a differentiable blur-formation objective.

The evaluation includes both a controlled synthetic benchmark and a purpose-built real capture system with synchronized short- and long-exposure cameras. This combination is valuable because synthetic data supplies controlled sharp references, while the eight-scene real dataset tests whether the approach transfers to genuine optical blur.

Improvements over the strongest reported two-stage baseline are substantial: PSNR rises from about 23.09 to 25.55 dB on synthetic data and from about 25.57 to 27.01 dB on real data, with consistent gains in SSIM and LPIPS. Qualitative examples also show sharper limbs, clothing boundaries, and facial details.

The ablations cover the principal design choices. Pose interpolation is especially well supported, while the experiments across blur magnitudes K=5,7,9,11 and the non-middle-timestep evaluation provide useful evidence that temporal regularization helps resolve motion direction rather than merely improving the central reconstruction.
weaknesses: The central sub-frame motion claim is not evaluated directly. On synthetic data, the authors could compare recovered joint trajectories, rotations, or vertices with the known sharp-frame motion. Image metrics alone cannot determine whether the method recovers correct motion or compensates for erroneous trajectories through avatar appearance and deformation parameters.

The claimed animatability is insufficiently demonstrated. Evaluation concerns novel views of the captured sequences, but there is no quantitative or convincing qualitative test on held-out poses, motion transfer, or reanimation. Thus, the evidence firmly supports blur-aware reconstruction, but not the broader claim of high-quality animation under novel motion.

Baseline breadth is limited to GauHuman and four 2D-deblurring-plus-GauHuman pipelines. No adapted 3D blur-aware reconstruction method or sharp-input oracle is reported. An oracle would quantify how much of the lost sharp-avatar quality is recovered, while a 3D-aware baseline would better isolate the advantage of the proposed human-motion model. The assertion that existing dynamic deblurring methods are inapplicable is not experimentally substantiated.

The physical formulation assumes uniform temporal sampling and direct averaging of rendered RGB values. The manuscript does not state whether averaging and losses operate in linear-radiance space; averaging gamma-encoded PNG/sRGB values would not match the stated photon-integration model. It also does not analyze exposure weighting, saturation, or temporal alignment between the short- and long-exposure real cameras.

Experimental reporting lacks per-subject/per-scene results, uncertainty, and statistical analysis. This matters for small ablation differences such as shape optimization on real data (27.010 versus 26.964 dB), which do not convincingly establish the importance claimed in the text. Results from only six synthetic subjects and eight real scenes also leave generalization to other clothing, motion, and backgrounds uncertain.

Reproducibility from the manuscript is weak despite the statement that code and data are public: it omits the architectures of the displacement and LBS-offset networks, loss weighting, optimization schedule and iteration count, initialization of spline controls, sampling details, and training cost. The real dataset also has inconsistent reported resolution—2080×2048 in the text versus 2448×2048 in Table 1—and the synchronization/exposure-center protocol is not specified.

The reliance on externally estimated SMPL poses and hard foreground masks is consequential, especially because motion blur corrupts both. The acknowledged foreground-background blending failure is therefore not merely cosmetic; it may bias supervision near fast-moving boundaries. Robustness to pose/mask errors is not measured.

Presentation needs refinement but is not decision-determining: the image/video-deblurring related-work discussion is substantially duplicated, several equations use ambiguous notation, Equation 17 names the combined objective as Lpho without an explicit regularization weight, and numerous grammatical errors remain.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and underexplored problem: reconstructing sharp, animatable 3D Gaussian human avatars directly from motion-blurred videos. Combining exposure-time rendering with an articulated human-motion prior is sensible and potentially useful.

The synchronized real-world benchmark is a meaningful contribution. Its four 50 ms blur cameras and eight 3.125 ms sharp cameras are center-time synchronized, enabling evaluation against real sharp observations from held-out viewpoints rather than only synthetic blur.

Results show substantial improvements over the reported baselines: from 23.080 to 25.546 dB on synthetic data and from 25.602 to 27.010 dB on real data, with similarly consistent SSIM and LPIPS gains. Qualitative examples also exhibit sharper contours and fewer motion artifacts.

The evaluation includes useful studies of blur magnitude, training-view count, pose-initialization perturbations, masks, temporal regularization, trajectory parameterization, and the number of virtual samples. The non-middle-timestep evaluation particularly supports the intended role of inter-frame regularization.
The manuscript is generally clear, motivates blur ambiguity well, and explicitly acknowledges limitations involving nonlinear sRGB averaging, geometry, loose clothing, and handheld objects.
weaknesses: The comparison set does not adequately establish the advantage over relevant 3D blur-aware reconstruction methods. The paper cites methods such as BARD-GS and DyBluRF but evaluates only GauHuman and pipelines coupling GauHuman with 2D deblurring. Even if existing dynamic methods are not directly animatable, comparisons or careful adaptations would help determine whether the gain comes specifically from the proposed human-aware formulation.

The main comparison is confounded: the proposed system jointly refines pose, shape, and LBS weights and uses a learned pose-deformation module, whereas the GauHuman baselines do not appear to receive comparable blur-aware motion optimization. Consequently, the reported gains do not cleanly isolate the contribution of exposure-time integration from that of a stronger pose-refinement pipeline. A sharp-input upper bound is also missing.

Several central implementation details are insufficient for reproduction. The architectures and inputs of the pose-displacement and LBS-offset CNNs are not specified, and the manuscript omits training iterations, initialization of the canonical Gaussians, sampling details, optimization schedules for the new variables, regularization details, and training time. The statement that code and data will be released does not resolve these omissions in the submitted manuscript.

Some claimed component benefits are weaker than presented. B-spline, Slerp, and linear trajectories differ by only about 0.01–0.11 dB, while removing shape optimization occasionally matches or slightly exceeds the full model, including at K_blur=9 and with two views. Thus the assertion that every component is necessary or that B-splines are clearly superior is not fully supported.

The real benchmark has eight scenes, but only aggregate scores are reported, without per-scene results, dispersion, or statistical analysis. The evaluation also relies on crops to estimated human bounding boxes without precisely defining whether identical crop regions and alignment are used across predictions and ground truth, which can materially affect all three metrics.

The physical model averages rendered sRGB values even though real exposure integrates linear radiance; the authors correctly acknowledge this, but it weakens the claim of a physics-based real-image formation model. The model also assumes appearance remains fixed while SMPL explains sub-frame motion, limiting its validity for cloth, hair, accessories, and other non-SMPL deformation.

There are technical and presentation ambiguities in the motion formulation: rotations are interpolated and additively displaced in a three-vector representation despite being described as elements of SO(3), the spline knot/boundary construction is not explained, and the inter-frame term is written as a geodesic distance between pose vectors without defining the rotation conversion. These issues leave uncertainty about the exact geometry being optimized.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically relevant and comparatively underexplored problem: reconstructing sharp, animatable Gaussian human avatars directly from motion-blurred multiview video. Combining differentiable blur formation with sub-frame SMPL motion optimization is a sensible contribution.

The evaluation includes both controlled synthetic data and a purpose-built real capture system with synchronized blurry and sharp cameras. Against the reported GauHuman-based baselines, the method obtains substantial improvements on both datasets (e.g., 25.546 versus approximately 23.08 dB on synthetic data and 27.010 versus at most 25.602 dB on real data).

The authors study blur magnitude, training-view count, pose-initialization perturbations, masks, trajectory parameterizations, and individual components. The inter-frame regularizer has particularly clear evidence on synthetic non-middle exposure times, improving PSNR by roughly 1.0–1.4 dB across the tested blur levels.

The manuscript is generally easy to follow, and it acknowledges important limitations involving nonlinear sRGB averaging, loose garments and handheld objects, and the inability of 3DGS to recover physically meaningful geometry.
weaknesses: The comparative evidence is too narrow to establish the claimed superiority of the overall approach. Every principal baseline uses GauHuman, either directly or after generic 2D deblurring. The paper does not evaluate other strong avatar backbones or blur-aware dynamic reconstruction methods such as DyBluRF or BARD-GS, despite discussing them. Consequently, the experiments do not separate the benefit of the proposed blur formulation from backbone choice or baseline adaptation quality.

Essential methodological and training details are absent. The manuscript does not adequately specify the canonical Gaussian-avatar construction, Gaussian initialization and densification, the architectures and inputs of the pose-displacement and LBS-offset CNNs, loss weights, iteration counts, temporal sampling, or how pretrained deblurring baselines are applied or fine-tuned. Referring only to the original 3DGS learning-rate schedule is insufficient for reproducibility, and the promised code and datasets are not presently available.

Several technical formulations are underdefined or physically inconsistent. Equation 1 omits exposure-time normalization while Equation 2 uses an average; rotations are interpolated and additively displaced as three-vectors without explaining the SO(3) parameterization or projection; the claimed geodesic regularizer is written as a norm of parameter-vector differences; and the paper never explains how the displacement network preserves valid rotations. These ambiguities make it difficult to assess whether the implementation matches the stated model.

The paper itself concedes that real blur is integrated in linear radiance whereas its model averages nonlinear sRGB renderings. This directly weakens the claim that the real-data method uses a physics-based blur model, particularly in saturated or high-contrast regions, yet no linearized-image experiment measures the effect.

Several component claims overstate the evidence. B-spline, Slerp, and linear trajectories are essentially tied, with differences around hundredths of a decibel; shape and LBS optimization provide very small or occasionally negative gains in Tables 3, 11, and 14. Thus the reported results do not support statements that these particular components are necessary or that B-splines are meaningfully superior.

Dataset and evaluation reporting is incomplete: the number of frames and train/test samples, per-subject or per-scene results, variability across runs, cropping protocol, and aggregation procedure are unspecified. Synthetic blur relies on RIFE-generated intermediate frames, but possible interpolation artifacts and the gap from real exposure integration are not analyzed.

The real-world generality claims are weakly supported. The custom dataset contains only eight scenes, novel-pose evaluation is qualitative, and the smartphone demonstration consists of a few images without ground truth or comparisons. The method also fundamentally depends on SMPL, limiting its applicability to loose clothing, accessories, and motion not represented by the body model.

Overall, the task and results are promising, but the restricted comparisons, incomplete technical specification, and unresolved formulation issues materially prevent the current manuscript from providing sufficiently reliable and reproducible support for acceptance.

strengths: The paper addresses a practical and underexplored problem: reconstructing sharp, animatable 3D Gaussian human avatars directly from motion-blurred multi-view video. Jointly modeling blur formation, sub-frame human motion, and the canonical avatar is well motivated and constitutes a meaningful computer-vision contribution.

The proposed 3D-aware formation model is conceptually sound: intermediate sharp renderings are generated by deforming a canonical Gaussian avatar with time-varying SMPL parameters and then averaged to reproduce the observed exposure. This makes better use of multi-view and human-body structure than an independent 2D-deblurring preprocessing stage.

The evaluation provides consistent evidence of effectiveness. The method improves substantially over GauHuman and four deblurring-plus-GauHuman pipelines on both synthetic and real data—for example, from roughly 23.1 to 25.5 dB on the synthetic benchmark and from 25.6 to 27.0 dB on the real benchmark, with similarly large LPIPS improvements.

The hybrid-exposure, time-synchronized 12-camera capture system is a particularly valuable aspect: blurry views serve as inputs while eight sharp views provide real captured novel-view references. This is stronger evidence than relying exclusively on synthetically averaged images.

The experimental study is broad within the proposed setting. It examines component ablations, temporal regularization, trajectory parameterization, knot and temporal-sample counts, pose-initialization perturbations, mask quality, blur magnitude, and training-view count. Results remain favorable as blur increases and views decrease.

The inter-frame regularizer is evaluated at non-middle exposure times, where motion-direction ambiguity actually matters. The sizeable improvements there support the stated motivation rather than merely showing a small aggregate metric gain.
Qualitative results indicate visibly sharper boundaries and finer body details, and the smartphone demonstration suggests potential usefulness beyond the controlled multi-camera setup.

The limitations section appropriately identifies important modeling restrictions, including averaging in nonlinear sRGB space and the inability of SMPL-driven motion to represent loose garments or handheld objects.
weaknesses: The strongest comparisons are limited to GauHuman and generic 2D video-deblurring methods followed by GauHuman. The paper does not compare with, or carefully discuss adaptations of, blur-aware dynamic NeRF/3DGS reconstruction methods cited in the related work. An oracle GauHuman model trained on the corresponding sharp inputs is also absent, making it difficult to assess how much of the remaining error comes from deblurring versus the underlying avatar model.

Reproducibility is weaker than the empirical breadth suggests. The pose-displacement CNN and LBS-offset CNN are not architecturally specified, the initialization and optimization of spline control parameters are only described coarsely, the relative weighting/scaling of the regularizer is unclear, and training duration, memory use, inference/rendering cost, and detailed schedules are not reported. A promised future code release does not substitute for manuscript-level specification.

The dataset protocols need greater precision. The manuscript reports six synthetic subjects and eight real scenes but does not give frame counts, motion composition, per-scene results, variance, or a clear aggregation protocol. Consequently, it is difficult to determine whether the reported gains are uniformly distributed or driven by particular subjects and motions.

The real benchmark supplies sharp reference images primarily around the exposure midpoint. Thus, it strongly validates midpoint novel-view appearance but cannot verify the recovered full sub-frame trajectory; the motion-direction evidence at non-middle times comes only from synthetic data.

Some motion-model details are technically under-justified. Rotations are represented and corrected additively in axis-angle coordinates despite living on SO(3), while the stated geodesic regularization is not explicitly formulated. The presented polynomial/matrix interpolation is called De Boor–Cox B-spline interpolation without specifying knots, degree, or boundary conditions, limiting both clarity and confidence in implementation equivalence.

Several ablated components provide only marginal gains, and some full-model numbers are slightly worse than simpler variants—for example, shape optimization at nine-frame blur and several two-view metrics. These do not invalidate the method, but claims that every component is necessary are stronger than the evidence supports.

The blur model assumes uniform temporal integration and averages rendered sRGB values. The authors acknowledge the latter limitation, but there is no experiment testing sensitivity to nonlinear camera response, rolling shutter, nonuniform exposure, or saturation, all of which matter for the paper's real-world framing.

Novel-pose animation and the monocular smartphone case are presented only qualitatively with very few examples. These results are encouraging demonstrations but do not substantiate broad generalization claims.

There are minor presentation issues, including calling Table 5 a “qualitative” ablation despite reporting quantitative metrics, grammatical errors, and an inconsistent normalization between the continuous blur equation and its discrete average. These are correctable and do not drive the rating.
